newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's petrol crisis may ease this week.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's petrol crisis may ease this week.

text.p: Bulgaria's interim transport minister said on Tuesday an alleviation of the country's severe fuel crisis was expected by the end of the week following a drastic hike of petrol prices.
The interim government raised petrol prices by up to 178 percent on Tuesday in a bid to free suppliers' volumes kept in storage.
"I hope that the fuel, which is hold back (by suppliers) will appear on the market...and by the end of the week we expect that the situation will be normal," Wilhelm Kraus told a news conference.
Kraus said more than 40 transport firms in the country did not have any fuel now and the cabinet had discussed on Monday a possibility for releasing fuel from the state reserve.
Most petrol stations in the country have been closed because of the fuel shortage.

Municipalities are distributing petrol and diesel for ambulances, food delivery trucks, the police, the army and social services, officials said. Bus transport in towns has been strongly reduced causing problems for industry, they added.

Shell Bulgaria, a Royal Dutch/Shell Group subsidiary and the only foreign fuel retailer in Bulgaria, which supplies its fuel only from the Neftohim refinery in Bourgas, said its all 23 petrol stations had no fuel.
"Our last fuel supplies were on February 8," Shell Bulgaria spokeswoman Kamelia Slaveikova told Reuters.

Petar Tsanov, deputy director of the biggest state-owned fuel retailer, Petrol, said the firm, which had 450 filling stations in the country, was receiving 150 tonnes of fuel per day while it needed 1,000 tonnes.

"The problem is in Neftohim's crude supplies and I expect that they will be regulated in two weeks," Tsanov said, adding that even if private firms freed fuel they had kept in storage such volumes would not be sufficient to solve the country's problem with the shortages.
The cash-stripped plant, which has been refining up to 9,000 tonnes of crude per day from 22,000 tonnes in December, needs credits to ensure crude supplies, officials said.

Neftohim, which is the country's biggest refinery supplying almost the whole domestic market with fuel, said on Tuesday it would increase the limited volumes by up to 400 tonnes per day to 1,500 tonnes of petrol and 1,000 tonnes of diesel.
The refinery, which owes millions of dollars to its crude suppliers, has 52,400 tonnes of crude on stock.

Neftohim expects a 61,500-tonne tanker from a private firm Yukos Bulgaria to arrive later on Tuesday at the Bourgas port from Russia's port of Odessa, Neftohim's spokeswoman Tatyana Hadzhieva said by telephone.

Last week the interim government, which inherited crippling fuel and grain shortages, banned fuel exports until April 30 and troops enforced border controls in a bid to curb oil smuggling by companies and private motorists to neighbouring countries, where fuel prices are higher.
Prime Minister Stefan Sofianski announced last Friday plans for partial privatisation of the debt-ridden Neftohim refinery but gave no further details.
